utterances.text: Well, as for what it would mean for such a person, I -- or such a body, I couldn't say, but it's quite obvious that the zone was not a demilitarised one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document, 1D962, please be admitted into evidence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is something I would like to correct, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it says "Amela [phoen], make a summary public." And then you have the initials "A.I" and not "A.J," this is the handwritten part. I know what the letter I in the Latin script looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see this document with this handwritten note before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Gajic's assistant showed it to me, but I'd never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to have a look at the heading of this document on the left side. Could it be zoomed in, please. Do you see a date there, and which one is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date and the time. The date, the 14th of July, 1995. Friday, 2229.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And below Republika Bosnia and Herzegovina you see another date, which one is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We see in the English translation the date of the 19th of July. And even the year was not translated or written down correctly. The reason for that could be the poor quality of the previous document or the copy of that document we have seen before and marked for identification as D102, so I think this translation needs to be checked again. Perhaps there are other mistakes. We can't simply attach this translation to the much better legible original document. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is exactly what the Defence has done. However, we are still waiting for the translation. And as soon as we get a correct translation of the document 1D962, we are going to upload it into the e-court. And you correctly observed that the previous document was of very poor quality and many elements therein were illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Therefore, this document will be marked for identification pending review of the translation. And that should apply, also, for D102. It's still marked for identification, but after a check of the translation it could be admitted at a later stage, too. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D962 shall be assigned Exhibit D349, marked for identification pending review of the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The document shall remain on the screen, and Judge Mindua has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Skrbic. This document 1D962, which became D349, I'd like to have another look at it. Have a look at item IV: "All persons who are fit for military service will be placed at the disposal of the Eastern Bosnia Light Brigade except for ..." and the sentence continues. Given your experience as a general, could you tell us whether this text says that these men fit for military service or -- had ipso facto become soldiers or members of the armed forces, or would it be necessary to have another document from the War Presidency? What is the actual situation that these individuals, these men find themselves in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it says here precisely that all those men fit for military service with work obligation are to be placed at the disposal of the 208 -- 65th Brigade, and without any additional conditions they become members of the brigade, they are issued weapons, their work obligation is terminated, and they become fully fledged members of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What does "work obligation" actually mean in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, "work obligation" means an obligation that involves any work to be performed without weapons; for example, toiling land or digging trenches, which was forbidden, but I know that they, in spite of that, did it. Now, everything that contained -- was contained in that work obligation and the people involved were just transferred from that status to the status of members of the armed forces and they are issued weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, according to this decision, were all people fit for work and military service placed at the disposal and engaged in defence with the exception of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this pertains only to able-bodied men. You asked me about people fit for work. I don't see from here who this referred to. This might be people over 65 years of age. But those who are fit for military service became members of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But in item III it says that all military persons -- persons fit for military --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir please repeat what it says in item III.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item III is different from item IV because under III it says: "All citizens fit for work will be put at the disposal of the civilian protection," not the brigade. Probably in anticipation of large-scale works to be done. So all people fit for work are placed at the disposal of that civilian protection. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were all the people fit for military service and for work placed at the disposal of the civilian protection and the defence within the region where a state of war had been proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Able-bodied are designated to be engaged in combat, whereas those fit for work are assigned to the civilian protection. And I think that the Trial Chamber understands what the tasks and duties and responsibilities of a civilian protection are, and that is something that is applicable all around the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir, please avoid overlapping. You start mostly too early with your next question. Now carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In order to avoid overlapping I am going to move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you were interviewed by the OTP, you were asked about the resubordination by the police to the army. Can you tell us now, according to what you know, was there any resubordination of the police to the VRS, and if so, how did that work?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, there was no resubordination ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please explain that in more detail. According to what you know, does it mean that it never happened or maybe you don't know about it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, police is resubordinated to the army only during a state of war and no specific document has to be issued to that effect because they become an integral part of armed forces. Because a state of war wasn't proclaimed in the territory of Republika Srpska up until the 20th of October, 1995, then my conclusion is that there had been no resubordination. They participated in joint actions - and that is the truth - but as adjacent units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Can you tell us -- do you know if members of the MUP were included in army units in the course of carrying out certain tasks?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were included but as a compact unit, not individually. They would report to the commander of an army unit, and they would carry out their task and, finally, report the Ministry of the Interior. If they were given any information from the commander, they received this information as their collaborators, and that was also the case vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic, for these answers. Now, can you tell me this: Was the Main Staff of the VRS endangered by the operations launched from the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we get some kind of time? This was a long war. And the last questions, I don't know even know if it had anything to do with Srebrenica. And we know that there was attacks coming out of those enclaves for a good while, so this doesn't help us, this kind of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you give us a time-frame?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The time-frame is one month prior to or after the events in Srebrenica. Or, Mr. McCloskey, you can take into account the whole war period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just want to get something the defendant -- excuse me, the witness can get his hands around. The events in Srebrenica. We need -- it's very simple to pick a date. The events in Srebrenica, according to us, went on for quite a long time, so that doesn't help us either for the witness. And -- but July 11th, when they came into Srebrenica, I mean, anything that would help the witness get a time-frame would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked Mr. Skrbic whether the Main Staff was endangered by the actions taken from the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves, and you can start from 1992 until the departure of the army from those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in order to respond to this question I am going to tell you how I obtained this information. Now, prior to my joining the Main Staff in 1994, I heard there had been attacks coming from Srebrenica, Zepa, targeting the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down when providing lots of information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the Han Pijesak-Crna Rijeka road, I also received information that workers at a petrol station had been killed. This petrol station was used by the Army of Republika Srpska, and it was in the village of Pod Plane, between Han Pijesak and Crna Rijeka, and this was also done by a sabotage group. When I came to the Main Staff, the basic command post was threatened on a daily basis by fire coming from mortars or other weapons. The rear command post in Han Pijesak was not in danger from those same directions. It was in danger from the direction of Pjenovac, which is in a completely opposite way. In addition to that, during the digging of trenches for water-pipes, General Mladic and I found a place on a hill where members of the BH Army had been staying, members from Zepa. We found a piece of paper, and then the commander told me, "You see, general, how seriously threatened we had been." In addition to that, Your Honour, the Crna Rijeka command post was fortified for defence. But in spite of that, our soldiers were being killed every day. Members of the protection regiment were recruits. They were not people who were drafted. And I am talking about young men between the ages of 17 and 21. This was particularly emotionally difficult for us. When expanded meetings of senior staff members with the commander of the Main Staff were being held, we would meet in an underground facility under the Zepa mountain particularly in order to avoid exposing ourselves to any danger. Around the command post, we had defence lines built with dugouts and trenches, and we had a round-the-clock combat duty service in those facilities. Now, these are these basic elements that indicate that there were armed operations coming from Zepa and Srebrenica and targeting the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, you said: "We found a piece of paper," and then the commander told me, "'You see, general, how seriously threatened we had been.'" Can you give us some more information about this piece of paper, about the content of this piece of paper, from where it came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't remember the contents of the piece of paper. I remember that there was a green background and there was a crescent. It shows that the Muslims had been present there. They had camped there. And he said that because we didn't know that they had been in that place, that they had stayed there, and they had stayed there because there was a pot that had remained there that they had used to cook food in. We knew that sabotage groups were infiltrating the area, but we didn't know that they had spent longer periods of time there. Three days, five days, half a month. Your Honours, I can't remember the details. I can tell you that I am sure that the VRS was not present there because we knew where our forces were deployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where did you find the piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 3 kilometres away on a hill above Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Since -- could you tell me that whether as a result of the sabotage activities in the Srebrenica and Zepa enclave, the Main Staff suffered any losses immediately prior to the events in Zepa? Are you familiar with anything of this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I have answered this question already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I had victims in mind, but I accept your answer.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were victims. There were victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the Main Staff have to take protective measures to protect from sabotage activity from Zepa and Srebrenica, from those two enclaves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Apart from what I have already mentioned in relation to the fortification of combat positions in the vicinity of the basic command post in Crna Rijeka, apart from that I could add that the 65th Protection Regiment and the 60th [as interpreted] Communications Regiment in addition to organising defence for the command post also organised patrols to which various tasks were assigned on various days. The tasks were very explicit. They were told which areas to patrol and what to control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we just check with the number of the communications regiment? I'm not sure we got the right translation there, or maybe ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, can you help us. You mentioned a protection regiment and a communications regiment. Can you tell us the numbers of these two regiments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the 67th Communications Regiment and the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Since you have already said something about where the rear command post was, could you tell us something about the security of the road that linked the basic command post and the rear command post where you were located?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, that road was one that General Djukic and I mostly used in the same vehicle. We went from Han Pijesak to Crna Rijeka and the other direction, too, at great risk. On one occasion, a patrol from the protection regiment prevented us from going to Crna Rijeka and we couldn't go there, but they said that there was a -- a risk of us losing our lives on that trip. General Mladic ordered, especially in 1995, that the police should escort us. So sometimes, when it wasn't urgent, we had a police escort. It was to provide combat security. It wasn't for transport purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Was this a normal way in which the Main Staff and its segments functioned in various areas or was that not the case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I believe that nothing is quite normal in -- in war. That it was essential, it was necessary, given the circumstances. Given all the dangers that were present, it was necessary for us to function in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you at the rear command post know which routes were used by the Muslims, and did you know where they organised ambushes from between those two places, the basic command post and the rear command post? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew about this. When General Mladic and I were returning from Banja Luka from a meeting with General Clark, we were in the same vehicle. And then, above Vlasenica, we stopped at a curve, a large curve, and the general then said, "Skrbic, I will take you to this cave now." There were mattresses in this cave, Your Honours. And he said Muslims from Zepa and Srebrenica have slept in this cave, and they continually used this road here, and they called it Allah's road, and that road linked Zepa and Srebrenica and Kladanj and Olovo, in fact. Since General Mladic showed me these paths, it's quite obvious that they used them. As for how they passed through and how they slept there, well, Your Honours, I am really not sure. We could have been at risk. They probably used these roads and these paths at night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. What did they call that road? It's not in the transcript. Could you tell them which road it is, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, and why it had the name that it had? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, General Ratko Mladic told me about the name, but he said that the Muslims had called the road "Allah's road."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Could you please repeat the name of the road because it hasn't been accurately recorded in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road of Allah, A-l-l-a-h. You can put it in inverted commas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have it on the record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber whether you had an opportunity to attend meetings with General Gvero, Tolimir, or Mladic, with foreign representatives or UNPROFOR representatives? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with UNPROFOR representatives but with the other representatives you have mentioned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you then tell us whether you attended meetings with the representatives of certain countries, certain foreign diplomats, and what could you tell us about such meetings?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Vlasenica, in mid-July 1995, there was a delegation from the Ukraine led by Mr. Alexander Alexandrovich, the diplomat Alexander Alexandrovich. The UNPROFOR battalion commander Lieutenant-Colonel Dudnjik joined him. And General Mladic, General Zivanovic, Colonel Skrbic - myself - and Jovica Karanovic, who was also a colonel, attended on behalf of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 59, lines 23 to 25, there are some names that aren't correctly recorded. Could the witness just repeat the names so that they can be correctly recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be helpful. Please repeat the names, slowly, you just have mentioned as participants of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll look at the English transcript. It will be easier for me. I am just looking at the names, because I can't understand anything else. Alexander Alexandrovich. Lieutenant-Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Stop. It was not -- sorry. It was not properly reported. Alexander Alexandrovich, without an A in the middle, Alexandrovich.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for having to say this. Alexandrovich. Perhaps it's difficult for you to pronounce but there is a difference between ch and ch, a soft ch and a hard ch. Alexandrovich.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have it now. And the other names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant-Colonel Dudnjik, that's correct. General Mladic. General Zivanovic. Colonel Skrbic, that's myself. I apologise to the interpreters. Colonel Skrbic, that's myself. Jovica Karanovic. That's correct now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Skrbic. Could you tell us something about how the meeting went and what subjects were discussed at the meeting since this is what you -- what you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of Mr. Tolimir's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the usual courtesies that are common in such circumstances, General Mladic said that the Muslims in Srebrenica and Zepa were obtaining weapons through the so-called parachute operation. It was said that they were also receiving weapons from the Ukraine. Alexander Alexandrovich claimed that they really were receiving weapons from the Ukraine but the -- but that the Ukraine wasn't trading in those weapons. General Mladic said that two members of the UNPROFOR battalion from the Ukraine had crossed over into the territory that was under the control of the VRS because they were under threat there. And Lieutenant-Colonel Dudnjik, the battalion commander, confirmed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's the time for a break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, I agree. We must have our second break and will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before the break, we have dealt with a document which was marked for identification under two different numbers. In the meantime, I noted that this document is part of the bar table motion of the Defence, I think of the first bar table motion, and therefore I would suggest that we decide about the admission, finally, by deciding pursuant to your bar table motion. Mr. Tolimir, please continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, you talked about the meetings in 1995. Now, during 1994, did you have an opportunity to be a member of any delegation from the Main Staff of the VRS that had meetings with representatives of foreign armies, UNPROFOR, and so on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us which ones?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of August, 1994, I was a member of a delegation led by General Ratko Mladic. We had a meeting with General Wesley Clark in Banja Luka. At the time, General Wesley Clark was an advisor to the president of the United States for defence. As far as I remember, with him was General Rose and another two generals, a major, a captain, and an interpreter, but I don't remember their names. In the VRS delegation were General Mladic, Naval Captain Beara, Colonel Skrbic - that's me - and an interpreter, Lieutenant-Colonel Kralj, and also General Zivomir Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, do you recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm afraid that the name of one of the participants is misspelled. Page 62, and the first name is wrong, but I'm not going to suggest anything to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, his first name is Zivomir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that correct now, Zivomir? Can you see that, line 4, page 63, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it. Yes, Your Honour, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means this General Zivomir Ninkovic took part, too. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, do you recall the content of those talks that you mentioned a minute ago. Do you recall anything about what was being discussed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, but I am going to tell you briefly what I remember best. General Wesley Clark told General Mladic that he had come to reach an agreement or to try to exert some influence for the contact group's plan to be adopted. In that respect, he highlighted a number of facts that would compel the VRS to accept the plan of the contact group. He told General Mladic that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had 450 tanks, 300 pieces of artillery, that it also had more troops than the Army of Republika Srpska. He also said that he was not going to go into how skilled they were, but they were obviously having larger numbers and that this was going to disrupt the balance of power and that eventually the Army of Republika Srpska would find itself in dire straits. He suggested to General Mladic, being an influential man and an experienced soldier, to do his best to have the plan accepted. He also threatened with bombing and invasion by NATO pact in order to provide support for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the event of the plan being rejected. Before that, General Mladic spoke about General Shalikashvili who was the chief of Joint Staff of the US Army, and he said that obviously he had his finger on the trigger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, it's very difficult for the interpreters to follow. Therefore, please slow down. You just said General Mladic spoke to a general from the US army. What was his name? That was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Wesley Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, and about another general. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, General Mladic spoke about General Shalikashvili. He said that he was the chief of the General Staff of the US Army. I don't know if that is correct, and I don't want to debate that. He also said that General Shalikashvili had his finger on the trigger. General Clark responded to that by saying that it wasn't fair for General Mladic to say that the chief of the General staff of the US Army had his finger on the trigger, and he brought to his attention the fact that NATO was prepared to start or become engaged in the war unless the plan of the contact group was accepted. Then Mr. Mladic asked him, "General, do you genuinely and honestly want to become involved in this war?" To which General Clark responded, "You will see what our reaction is going to be." If I may add one more sentence, Your Honours, General Clark claimed that their assessment was there was not the balance of power in Bosnia-Herzegovina until 1995 and that he would do his best in order to restore this balance of power or, rather, that the balance be tipped to the advantage of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, as for other pleasantries that were exchanged at the meeting, I don't think there is any need to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Can you tell us this: At the time, did General Clark perform any duties within the peacekeeping force, or was he strictly a US army general? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I explained that the duty of General Clark was to act as an advisor to the president of the United States and the Congress, and I don't think he had any other role. That is how he was introduced to us at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. And did NATO indeed become involved in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the former SFRY as announced by General Clark while he was an advisor to the president of the USA? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Mr. Gajic, what is this SFRY?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't know why you are putting a question to Mr. Gajic. Just continue, Mr. Tolimir. It's not a proper question to you, Mr. Gajic. We all know what SFRY is. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we correct the translation? I did not speak about the SFRY. I spoke about the USA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can Mr. Skrbic now answer this question: Did NATO take part only on the side of one of the warring parties or was it involved on both sides? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO provided close air support to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as to the Croatian Army who carried out an offensive against Republika Srpska. Close air support involves reconnaissance, electronic support, bombing, and transportation. In addition to that, they provided support through artillery and artillery ammunition. In 1996, above the village of Pecka, situated near Mrkonjic Grad and Mliniste, I managed to identify a firing position that had been used by artillery, and its shell casings had NATO numbers on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Since we were discussing NATO, did you have an opportunity to attend any other meeting with representatives of NATO members? Thank you. Representatives of NATO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. I think this was already in 1996, when I was ordered by General Mladic to join you and that we go to the Jela to conduct talks with Admiral Leighton Smith. He was, at the time, the commander of NATO forces in Europe. I remember that the admiral told us that their role was to establish the balance of power between the Army of BiH on the one hand and the VRS on the other. When I made a remark to the effect that this balance was disrupted to extreme detriment to the Army of Republika Srpska, the admiral responded, respectfully, that that was the outcome and the result of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Can you please repeat the full name of General Smith because it was not recorded properly in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Admiral Leighton Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. General Clark and General Leighton Smith, with whom you had talks in 1994, did they later become representatives of the USA amongst the ranks of UNPROFOR or SFOR who were deployed in the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember anything else with regard to the meeting with Mr. Leighton Smith?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it is important for you, Your Honours, I can say that the admiral told us that he was going to spend his next weekend in Rome. But before that, he would be flying by helicopter to Split, and then board a military plane there and spend some time with his wife after that. The admiral asked us, "Where are you going to spend your weekend?" And the General Tolimir responded, "On the mountain." After the meeting ended, they gave an interview for a television station, but I did not participate in that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. I would like to clarify something. What is the rank of Mr. Leighton Smith? Or was at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had the rank of admiral and he was dressed in a naval uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You said this meeting at the Jela restaurant took place in 1996. Do you recall which month or day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that Mr. Tolimir was a participant of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you understood me correctly. Mr. Tolimir led a delegation and I was part of that delegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who else from the Main Staff of the VRS took part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that only the Lieutenant-Colonel Kralj who acted as an interpreter was also present, and then the technicians, Your Honour, who were helping with technical issues, naturally, but they didn't participate in the discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we now see P1011 on the screen. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, as we can see, the title of this document is: "Agreement on Complete Cessation of Hostilities." And in the first line we can see the date when the document was signed. Could you tell us when it was signed, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was signed on the 23rd of December, 1994. Your Honour, I have a problem with my glasses. The lens has fallen out, but I hope I will be able to read this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can the Court Usher assist in any way --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- so that we are able to continue? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can see that a little screw has fallen out and so we have got a job for the witness section, and obviously his glasses are important, but I leave this in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I think we should use the remaining 15 minutes of today's hearing in that way that you put questions to the witness without directing him to specific parts of the documents. And I hope, very much, that the problem will be resolved during this afternoon so that we can continue in a normal way tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will read it out. The title of the document is: "Agreement on Complete Cessation of Hostilities." The first sentence reads as follows: "Following the cease-fire agreement signed on the 23rd of December, 1994, the parties agreed to a complete cessation of hostilities with effect from 1200 hours on the 1st of January, 1995 ..." And this concerns all the lines of confrontation. Since agreement on cease-fire is mentioned in the first sentence and in the second line reference is made to cessation of hostilities, could you tell us what the difference is between a cease-fire and a cessation of hostilities? What is covered by the term "cease-fire" and what by the term "cessation of hostilities"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A cease-fire means that the units on both sides remain at their combat positions but they cease to open any kind of fire. A cessation of hostilities, however, means establishing a peace through a gradual process of withdrawing the units and troops from their respective combat positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Given what you have said and what we have just read out, were you aware of the fact that this agreement on cessation of hostilities had in fact been agreed, had in fact been reached?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll read out the second sentence now. "This agreement will remain in effect for an initial period of four months, subject to renewal under these same conditions with the agreement of the parties concerned." Thank you. Was the witness [as interpreted] cease-fire respected?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the agreement on a cessation of hostilities respected, given that the agreement on a cease-fire was not respected?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the cease-fire wasn't respected and that entailed a failure to respect the agreement on a cessation of hostilities as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know who violated the agreement on the cessation of hostilities? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Muslim side violated both agreements with the authorisation of the president, Alija Izetbegovic, and then the VRS responded. So neither side respected the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you a participant at the meetings of the Main Staff when this subject was discussed and information pertaining to the subject was provided? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did attend some of the meetings of the collegium or the meeting of the commanders of the Main Staff of the VRS, and at those meetings we were provided with a brief information, but at some meetings we were provided with detailed information. This information was usually provided by Colonel Petar Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive any information, any intelligence information, signed by Tolimir or Salapura? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, at the rear command post, as far as I can remember we didn't receive any such information. But when General Djukic and myself went to Crna Rijeka in the operations centre, it was possible for us to obtain such information. So I, personally, made some notes with regard to this intelligence information. I didn't copy everything. I made some notes for my own personal use and in order to be able to inform members of the sector for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it possible for you and General Djukic to have access to all intelligence information when you required such information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we didn't make such requests very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Given the access to information that you had when you arrived at the command post, could you, on that basis, determine the level of reliability of the information pertaining to certain events? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the way the war developed in the territory of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, about 90 per cent of the intelligence information was, in fact, confirmed. It was confirmed by the events in those territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that intelligence in 1993 and 1994 [as interpreted], did you find out certain things about the way in which the Muslims armed themselves? And the period of time I referred to was 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I haven't fully understood your question. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive intelligence about Muslims arming themselves in the course of the year 1994 and 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, information about Muslims arming themselves could be found in that information or we would be orally informed of the fact at the meetings in the manner that I have just described, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Could you please tell us, at the beginning of 1995, did the Main Staff have any information on plans for the ABiH and the Croatian Army launching large-scale combat operations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. The Main Staff had reliable information concerning the ABiH and the Croatian Army launching an attack on the western part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And that information that you had at your disposal, was that information subsequently confirmed by the way in which the events unfolded?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered that question. Unfortunately, almost 90 per cent of the information that we had was confirmed by the subsequent wartime events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now have a look at 1D1111. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here on the screen we can see the notes that you made in the course of the war. As you don't have your glasses, could you please tell us how this document was created? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document consists of my own personal notes that were made from the 18th of March, 1995, until about the month of May of that same year. O stands for "operative," and this represents some of the notes that I personally made for myself. Everything that concerned areas outside the sector were marked with this letter O, and this shows that it's an authentic document that I, myself, created because no one in the VRS or in the Main Staff made such notes. O1, O2, and so on and so forth are markings that I used because my intention was to add to these paragraphs at a later date or to use them for research purposes. I haven't done any of that yet. This document is an authentic one from that year. Although it was typed on a computer, there is nothing that I added or deleted from the document. Whatever I added I would mark. I'd use my initials. I'd mark such sections with my initials, PS, and that is how one proceeds in scientific works.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On what basis of what information did you compile these notes? Could you please tell us that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made these notes on the basis of intelligence from the Main Staff and on the basis of the oral presentations made at the meetings of the Main Staff commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A while ago you answered this question partially, so I apologise for repeating my question. After these notes had been made, did you amend these documents in any way? Did you add anything to the document or to the notes or did you comment on these notes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have to come to an end for today, but let me put a final question to the witness. I would like to know if you -- what we can see on the screen, if that is the original version of your notes, or did you make your notes by handwriting or how was it done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had a laptop computer while working in the sector. Sometimes I would take the laptop to the command post in Crna Rijeka, and then I would directly enter this information into the laptop. When I didn't have the laptop on me, I would make notes in a notebook. And when I would then return to Han Pijesak to the rear command post, I would transfer the information to a computer, and I would then simply destroy or get rid of the handwritten notes. So this is the electronic version of my notes, the digital version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. I am quite sure that you are going on tomorrow dealing with this document, but for today we have to finish our hearing. We adjourn and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom. And again, no permission to contact either party during the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
